$comment: What was read, and at which revision, for every column of the comparison table in README.md.
The table is the one thing this project ships that makes claims about other people's software,
and it goes wrong without anything breaking. `npm run smoke` already checks how OLD it is;
this file makes it checkable whether the other side has MOVED since we looked, which is the
question that actually decides whether a cell still holds. `npm run table-sources` compares
each `sha` against that project's current HEAD and names the columns worth re-reading.
Adopted from csitte.at, whose rule is 'no matrix cell without our own evidence' — they record
the foreign HEAD before mirroring a row. On 2026-08-26 their recorded SHA for taylorwilsdon
and ours matched, which is how a claim about a third party should be confirmable at all.
The README's `comparison-table-verified` marker carries the OLDEST `verified` date in this
file, not the newest, and a test enforces exactly that. A table is only as current as its
stalest column; tying the marker to the newest check would let one freshly re-read column
stand in front of the others and — since the age budget in `npm run smoke` is measured from
that same marker — reset the budget for all of them. On 2026-09-07 the taylorwilsdon column
alone moved the marker from 09-03 to 09-07, which is what prompted the rule. So: pulling one
column forward no longer re-dates the table, and the columns that hold the marker back are
named in the test failure.
`shaBasis` is deliberately part of the record: `recorded` means the SHA was read at the time
of checking, `inferred` means it was reconstructed afterwards from the commit history (safe
only when the repository did not move between the check and the reconstruction). Never write
`recorded` for a SHA nobody wrote down — that is the exact habit this file exists to break.

First reading of this column, added on 2026-09-08 — the date we read, at the revision the repository stood at. It was found by a landscape scan rather than by any cell moving, and the finding is about our own selection: at 176 stars it is an order of magnitude larger than the klodr column we already carried, actively maintained, TypeScript, Apache-2.0. It had been passed over because it is a Workspace suite rather than a Gmail server, which is a reason to describe it carefully, not a reason to omit it. Read at this revision: src/factory/manifest/gmail.yaml end to end (fifteen Gmail operations — search, read, archive, send, reply, replyAll, forward, triage, trash, untrash, getAttachment, viewAttachment, modify, labels, threads, getThread — so send, reply and forward are all present), src/factory/safety.ts, src/accounts/credentials.ts, src/server/batch.ts. The send row is the one that made this column worth adding: safety.ts defines a `draft-only-email` policy blocking send/reply/replyAll/forward, and a `no-delete` policy blocking permanent deletion — the only other server on this table that will refuse to send at all. Both are opt-in through GWS_SAFETY_POLICY, so the default is a sending server and the promise is an operator's environment variable, which is why the cell reads `sends` first. Bulk is by explicit ids, not by query: batch.ts maps `users.messages.batchModify` over `items` carrying a messageId (`ids: items.map(...)`), with no query path anywhere. `triage` is a fixed `messages.list` with `q: 'is:unread in:inbox'` plus a per-message hydration walk — a list, with no bucketing or aggregate stats, hence the qualified cell rather than a tick. `search` is `messages.list` with hydration via `messages.get` at format=metadata; the returned labels are never re-checked against the query, so the re-verification cell is a dash. It goes through messages.list rather than threads.list, which is the endpoint our own measurement found the drift in — worth recording, because it means the cell describes a missing check and not an observed failure. No unsubscribe, no snooze, no filter tool: `snooze`, `unsubscribe`, `Authentication-Results`, `dkim` and `dmarc` have no hit in the repository, and the only occurrence of `filter` in gmail.yaml is a comment — `users.settings.filters.*` appears solely in src/google/descriptor.json, which is the generated catalogue of what Google offers, not of what the server registers. No output_schema or outputSchema anywhere. credentials.ts writes the token as plain JSON at mode 0600 with no cipher, so the encryption cell is a dash like the other community columns. The least-privilege cell names something genuinely different from ours and worth watching: ADR-202 records a per-ACCOUNT read/readwrite level, and safety.ts enforces it at call time against the scopes Google actually granted — read from the credential file, checked against Google's own per-method scope list in the generated descriptor rather than a hand-kept table. Its direction is the same as ours; its position is later, at the call rather than at registration.
